concepts.title: What Are Rights? Claims Backed by Society and Law
concepts.definition: A right is a claim that a person is entitled to make on society -- to speak, to practise a faith, to move freely -- which the community and its laws recognise and are bound to respect. Rights supply what one cannot secure alone: a social guarantee that one's vital interests will be honoured.
concepts.key_idea: Rights are entitlements, not favours -- claims others are obliged to honour.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps105.txt lines 1-90 (introduction, definition of rights as claims, rights as necessary conditions for a dignified life)
question_patterns: define rights and explain their essential features
in class 11 rights chapter: how does a claim become a right
why are rights described as claims on society
distinguish a right from a privilege or a favour
what makes rights necessary for a dignified life
give an example of a right and the duty it imposes on others

solution_steps.explain: Spot what the person demands -- a liberty, a service, non-interference -- and whether it serves a basic interest.
A claim becomes a right when law and social practice acknowledge it and assign matching duties to others.
Because rights are enforceable, their holders can appeal to courts and public opinion when they are denied.

concepts.title: Where Rights Come From: Natural, Historical and Legal Bases
concepts.definition: Thinkers ground rights differently: as natural rights inhering in human beings before any state; as historical gains won through long struggles, from Magna Carta to freedom movements; or as legal rights created and listed by constitutions. Most modern theorists blend these -- rights are human claims given shape by history and guaranteed by law.
concepts.key_idea: Born as moral claims, hardened by struggle, sealed by law -- rights carry all three ancestries.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps105.txt lines 90-170 (natural rights, historical evolution of rights, legal rights and constitutional guarantees)
question_patterns: what are natural rights and who proposed this view
in class 11 rights chapter: how did historical struggles shape rights
distinguish natural legal and moral rights
why do rights need constitutional recognition
trace the historical development of the idea of rights
can a right exist before the law recognises it

solution_steps.explain: Lockean thought treats life, liberty and property as prior claims no government may cancel.
Rights like the vote were won through struggle, expanding from property-owning men to all adults.
Constitutions convert moral and historical claims into enforceable legal rights.

concepts.title: Rights and Duties: The Two Sides of One Claim
concepts.definition: Every right implies duties: my freedom of speech obliges others to tolerate my expression, while my rights survive only inside a society where I too perform my obligations -- respecting others' identical rights, obeying just laws, contributing to common resources.
concepts.key_idea: A right on one side is a duty on the other -- claim and obligation are one relation seen twice.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps105.txt lines 170-240 (rights and duties, why duties accompany rights, mutual respect among right holders)
question_patterns: explain the relationship between rights and duties
in class 11 rights chapter: what duties follow from my right to speak freely
can a person enjoy rights while ignoring all duties
whose duty corresponds to a child's right to education
why must right holders respect the rights of others
give one right and list the duties it creates for the state and citizens

solution_steps.explain: For every right, ask who must do or refrain from what -- that duty is the right's other face.
Rights work only within a law-abiding community, so each holder also owes general duties of cooperation.
A society of pure claimants collapses; duties keep the system of rights stable and fair.

concepts.title: Rights in a Democracy and Their Political Importance
concepts.definition: Rights make democracy real for each person: they protect dissent between elections, secure the free information votes depend on, and shield minorities from majority whims. A democracy without enforceable rights can be majoritarian pressure dressed as rule by the people.
concepts.key_idea: Elections choose rulers; rights keep them civilised between elections.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps105.txt lines 240-320 (rights in a democracy, why rights are needed for democratic participation, protection of minorities and dissent)
question_patterns: why are rights essential for the working of democracy
in class 11 rights chapter: how do rights protect minorities from the majority
what would elections look like without freedom of expression
how do rights keep power accountable between elections
explain the link between rights and political participation
can a democracy survive if rights of dissenters are crushed

solution_steps.explain: Speech, association and movement are the inputs democracy runs on; rights guarantee them against suppression.
Constitutional rights bind majorities too, so losing a vote never means losing one's standing as a citizen.
Free press and protest expose misrule continuously, keeping elected power answerable.

concepts.title: Rights of the Accused, and the Right to Resist
concepts.definition: Rights extend even to those suspected of crimes: fair trial, legal defence and protection from torture mark a civilised system, for guilt must be proved, not presumed. And when a state turns systematically tyrannical, political theory recognises a residual right to resist -- the warrant behind struggles against colonial and dictatorial rule.
concepts.key_idea: Justice is measured at its margins -- by the rights of the accused and by when resistance becomes legitimate.
concepts.textbook_ref: keps105.txt lines 320-400 (rights of accused and arrested persons, right against torture, right to constitutional remedies, right to resist tyranny)
question_patterns: which rights protect a person accused of a crime
in class 11 rights chapter: why is the right against torture non-negotiable
when does a right to resist unjust rule arise
why must guilt be proved in a court rather than assumed
explain the right to constitutional remedies
how do fair trial rights protect society as a whole

solution_steps.explain: Presumption of innocence, fair and speedy trial, counsel of choice and freedom from torture guard the suspect.
These protections keep the state honest; punishing the unproven corrupts every citizen's security.
When legal channels are destroyed by tyranny, theory concedes a right of resistance, exercised as a last resort.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A citizen demands freedom of speech but heckles every meeting he disagrees with. Analyse the inconsistency using the rights-duties framework.

solution_template.explain: He may speak and publish -- a right others must respect.
The same right obliges him to leave others' speech unmolested; heckling denies them what he claims.
Rights are reciprocal; he may protest outside the hall, but silencing speakers breaks the duty attached to his own right.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A mob catches a suspected thief and wants instant punishment without trial. Explain which rights are at stake and why the state insists on a trial.

solution_template.explain: The suspect's rights to fair trial, counsel and protection from violence are all in danger from mob punishment.
Accusation is not proof; only a court testing evidence can establish guilt.
Trial rights protect everyone, since any citizen could one day face a false accusation.

questions: What are rights and why are they called claims on society?
